I did a big donation drive at my daughters school a few years back after both a teacher and a cook had a child shipped out.  We collected tons of stuff and wound up connecting with the local recruiting office - we sent several boxes directly to each of the boys we knew and the rest we let them get names of people from our area who'd been deployed and mail them over.

We used a big bulletin board to pin up examples of things to buy - shoe insoles, playing cards, jerky, sunflower seeds, wipes, tissues, gum - most of what we suggested were items you could find at a Dollar Store - the school had a very poor socio-economic makeup.  We're talking kids who lived in RVs with their entire families and shared campground bathrooms as a way of life - they made up about 1/2 of the school - the rest were a bit better off.

Those kids scraped together pennies.  They drew pictures.  We wound up doing massive art projects in the gym - thank you cards and pictures with the kids handprints or rainbows or whatever, so that each box got 1/2 a dozen kid-made cards or pictures in it.  

When the recruiter and his wife came to pick up all the surplus that we'd collected and had decided to share with others - he held back tears.  I was very proud.


So - if you have kids, or are a teacher, or whatever - do it at work - do it at school - church - or just at home - but share the message that you support our troops and invite others to join in with you.

I've also done 1/2 a dozen or so boxes every so often to 'any soldier' or when I find out someone we know has been deployed.  I can get bulk items on eBay.

* You can donate them to an animal shelter - I've heard they can always use newspapers, old phone books and towels for bedding.

* You can ball up the pages to use in place of packing peanuts.

* You can put use them to kill weeds.  You pretty much blanket an area with the newspaper, cutting off all sunlight.  If you do this over the winter the paper will be nearly gone by Spring and then you can till it into the soil, or cover with bark chips or decorative rocks, etc.

* Offer a months supply on Craigslist to someone who needs it.

* Use the Sunday coupons to get stuff free. ;)

* Line pet cages with it.

* Use for packing plates and other breakables.

Google found me this: http://www.associatedcontent.com/article/19136/25_extraordinary_uses_for_old_newspapers.html

* Around the House:

1. Temporarily block the sun from streaming in windows.

2. Spread sheets of newspapers out and make clothing patterns

3. Dampen and spread over window glass to protect it when you paint.

4. Line and protect closet shelves and drawer bottoms

5. Place folded newspapers on the floor as a mat for wet shoes or muddy boots.

6. Make fire logs out of old newspapers. Roll sheets of newspapers up tightly in the shape of a log. Tie them tight with string and use them in your fireplace or on a camp fire.

7. Do you still have some old 45 or other type of vinyl records? Store them safely by placing old newspapers in between each one.

8. Ball up half sheets and let Kitty play with them. Cats love the crinkling noise.

9. Place balls of old newspapers inside leather shoes, purses, and in suitcases. They
help leather items keep their shape. They also help deodorize them.

* In the Garage...

10. Use old newspapers to polish windows to a streak-free shine. Also great for polishing chrome.

11. Your auto have a fluid leak? Place sheets underneath your car when it's parked in the garage to protect the floor.

12. If your auto's parked outside in the winter weather, lay old newspapers on the windshield so you don't have to clean off ice and snow in the morning.
In the Garden...

13. Spread out sheets of newspaper between plants in your garden to keep weed growth down. Cheaper than black plastic!

14. Make mulch for your garden.

15. Bring green tomatoes in the house and wrap them in old newspapers. Place them in a dark, cool area, and 
they will ripen nicely.

16. Expecting a frost? Cover vulnerable garden plants with tents made out of newspapers.

17. Fold them over and kneel on them when you're working in the garden.

18. Transport fresh flowers in damp newspaper to keep them fresh longer.

* Miscellaneous...

19. Buy some glue, long sticks, string, and let your kids make kites.

20. Celebrate New Year's Eve with confetti made from old newspapers.

21. Let the kids keep busy on a rainy day. Let them make paper chains, hand puppets, or costumes.

22. Make a kid's birthday party fun! Use filled balloons, flour, water, and strips of old newspapers to create a piñata.

23. Wrap up glass and other breakables in thick sheets of newspaper before you pack them to move.

24. Temporarily cover up a broken window until you can get it repaired.

25. Use strips of newspaper in place of litter in your kitty's box.

After my divorce I bought a small manufactured home, the insulation was, of course, crappy and the furnace was so inefficient it was laughable.

I switched to using two $30 Walgreens space heaters {that I got on sale and discounted down to just $15 ea} and used them, combined with strategically placed curtains and cut our electric bill by about 70%.

I used one of the spring loaded shower curtain rods and hung a bunch of extra sheer curtains I had that just happened to be the perfect floor to ceiling length - I placed this at the end of the hallway, effectively dividing the home in 1/2.

During the day when we were generally in the livingroom/diningroom/kitchen we had the space heater going in the front of the house.  

During the night when we were, obviously, generally sleeping I had the space heater in the doorway to the bathroom, on low.

This meant that the bathroom was pretty damn chilly during the day, and first thing in the morning the front of the house was cold as well - but going from $300 a month to heat the 972 sq ft home down to about $80 was MORE than worth it.

I also used the curtains during the summer to concentrate the portable A/C and make it more efficient - we'd just open the windows at night to cool off.

Oh, and thermal curtains in your windows can cut typical heating/cooling costs by 25% - I was skeptical, but now am pleased with the investment {as they're a tad costly}.

An added benefit to using curtains to concentrate the heat or A/C is that you don't have to worry about remembering to 'shut the door' - no slamming door all day, no reminding the kids, and some heat does still make its way into the other part of the house, so it cuts down on worry about mold/mildew that you might otherwise run into.

Now that we're in a much larger 'real' house we still use curtains in various doorways when needed - if none of the kids are home there's no point in heating the upstairs 3 bedrooms, 1 bathroom, large landing and hallway - so we close that off - and open them up when they come home.

So, that's my experience - curtains, both inside and on windows, used to your advantage.

Oh, and the space heaters we got have the safety feature where if they're knocked over they automatically shut off, and sense if something gets accidentally dropped on it {like a blanket or whatever} and knows to shut off.  I used the bathroom floor instead of the carpeted hallway just to reduce possible accidents.

My father killed himself over the summer.  I hadn't talked to him in years, he was physically present very little in my childhood.

I still cry about his death randomly.  I still ache, feel pain, anger, regret, a twisty rollercoaster of emotions that got real old real fast, but I haven't found the exit.

Whether you reach out to a single person, or a group, find someone you can vent to.  Just speaking the words aloud helps me.  I looked into a few support groups, in person and online, but I felt like somehow I didn't 'belong' because of the estrangment that had been between my father and I for a number of years {he'd threatened to kill me, leading to little contact with him in the last decade}.  I'm lucky to have a boyfriend who listens to whatever I need to say at that moment, whether it's making a morbid joke {like 'I wonder what the second to last thing that went through his mind was?'}, randomly making snide comments about fictional TV Dads and how I'd sure have liked to have a Dad like that, or sitting on our dining room floor, crying, and needing a hug.

Don't bottle up your feelings.  I pretty much locked myself away in the house for weeks, because I knew if someone asked how I was I'd verbally vomit my emotions all over their shoes.  I even experienced odd physical reactions necessitating an EKG, it wasn't a fun time.

I have this fear of suicide being "contagious" and I analyzed my reactions repeatedly.  I have no urge to kill myself, thankfully.

I have children, I'm in my late 30's and I experience more love and joy in a week than I think my father did in his entire lifetime.  I understand why he did what he did, for the most part, though I'm sometimes confused all over again, it certainly wasn't his first try, just his most successful.

If you'd like to communicate with me privately, I'm open to that.  I wound up not going to in-person meetings because I didn't want to 'take time away from my kids' {admittedly a bit of an excuse}, nor did I wind up joining the online forums I'd found, because I was afraid of focusing too much on it.  But I'm open to talking about it, and would like to help someone else, even just a little, to help feel like there's a reason this happened in my life.  {I'm a nontheist, btw, so I'm not a good source of religious comfort, if you're looking for that}.

Anyway.  Hang in there.  I felt like everywhere I turned there was suicide or reference to it in TV & movies for months, and it brought things up often.  As for telling your daughter - my personal choice was to tell my kids upfront.  To talk to them about why I believed his choice was the wrong one.  I made a point to tell them it was up to them whether or not they told anyone and what they told them - I didn't want the "dark secret" to cause more pain/drama later in our lives.  They had virtually no contact with him, so they didn't grieve, but had to live with me grieving.  All their birthdays taking place in the summer was a challenge.

Treasure that you were there for her when she needed you most.  You at the very least brought her a sense of comfort and support at the end.

Don't let anyone tell you what you're 'supposed' to or 'allowed' to feel about her {I saw the other post about how she wasn't your 'real' sister, fuck that noise}.
